dryRun.title: What counts as extra space?
rows: a Set of up to n values
dryRun.note: The third function creates no array at all, but it still costs O(n), because each waiting call sits on the call stack.

think.q:
let depth = 0, max = 0
function down(n) {
  depth++
  max = Math.max(max, depth)
  if (n > 0) down(n - 1)
  depth--
}
down(5)
console.log(max)
why: The calls are down(5), down(4), ... down(0). That is 6 calls waiting at the same time, so the stack is 6 frames deep.
The depth grows with n, so the space is O(n) even though no array is created.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
const b = a
const c = [...a]
b.push(4)
console.log(a.length, c.length)
why: const b = a copies nothing: a and b are the same array, so the push shows in both. That costs O(1) space.
[...a] really copies all n items, which costs O(n) space. That is why c stays at 3.
think.exec:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
const b = a
const c = [...a]
b.push(4)
console.log(a.length, c.length)

think.q: A function reverses an array in place, using only two index variables. What is its extra space?
why: Two integers are enough, however long the array is. The input array is not counted.
Trap: counting the input itself. Only memory the function creates counts.

think.q: A function returns arr.map(x => x * 2). What is its extra space?
why: map builds a brand-new array with n items. That new array is memory the function created, so the space is O(n).
Trap: thinking a one-line function must be O(1).

think.q: Two Sum can be solved with two nested loops, or with a hash map. Which statement is true?
opts: The hash map is better in time and in space
Nested loops: O(n²) time and O(1) space. Hash map: O(n) time and O(n) space
why: The hash map spends memory to save time. This trade is the most common one in algorithms.
Always state time and space together, because improving one often costs the other.

try.task: Write reverseInPlace(arr). Reverse the array in place with O(1) extra space and return the same array. Do not create a second array.
examples: const a = [1, 2, 3]; reverseInPlace(a)  // a is now [3, 2, 1]
try.hint: Use two indexes, one at each end. Swap the two items, then move both inward until they meet.

checks.t: returns the same array, not a copy
checks.verify: const a = [1, 2]; assert(reverseInPlace(a) === a, "must return the same array")

takeaway.key: Space complexity counts only the extra memory you create, and that includes the call stack. The input does not count.
mistakes: Counting the input array as part of your space.
Forgetting the call stack: a recursion n levels deep costs O(n).
Thinking b = a makes a copy. It only shares the same array.
Reporting time and forgetting to say what the speed-up costs in memory.

dryRun.title: The five steps on "does this array contain a duplicate?"
rows: Restate the task. Ask about empty arrays and about the values.
Return true if any value appears twice. An empty array gives false.
Write small cases, including the edges.
Say the simplest way that is surely correct.
Compare every pair: O(n²) time, O(1) space
Find the repeated work. The question is "have I seen this before?"
A Set remembers values: O(n) time, O(n) space
Write it, then run your examples through it.
All three examples give the expected answer
dryRun.note: Step 3 is the base line and step 4 improves it. You can only say what you improved if you first said what the slow version costs.

think.q: Why do you write small examples before writing any code?
opts: To prove the problem is easy
To find out early whether you understood the task, and to have tests ready
why: Examples turn a vague statement into something you can check. A wrong idea shows up in seconds, not after twenty lines of code.
They also become your tests in step 5.

think.tag: Catch the bug with an example
think.q:
Your example says [1, 2, 3] must give false. What does this code print?

function hasDup(a) {
  const s = new Set()
  for (const x of a) {
    s.add(x)
    if (s.has(x)) return true
  }
  return false
}
console.log(hasDup([1, 2, 3]))
why: The code adds the value before checking, so every value finds itself and the function returns true at once.
A tiny example such as [1, 2, 3] exposes this in step 5. Without it the bug can hide.

think.q: You have described a brute-force solution and its cost, O(n²). What is the best next move?
opts: Code it right away and stop
Ask the interviewer to give the answer
Memorise a famous trick for this problem
Ask what work is repeated and what you know but are not using yet
why: Optimizing means finding repeated work or unused information: sorted input, a value you keep searching for, a result you keep recomputing.
The brute force gives you a correct answer to compare against.

think.q: Which question belongs to step 1, Understand?
opts: Can the array be empty, and can values repeat?
Which data structure should I use?
Does my code pass the tests?
why: Step 1 is about the problem: its input, output and rules.
The other questions belong to later steps: complexity (3 and 4), data structure (4) and testing (5).

think.q: You already have [1, 2, 3, 1] (true) and [1, 2, 3] (false). Which example adds the most?
opts: Another array of different positive numbers
The same array in reverse order
A longer array of distinct numbers
why: The empty array is a boundary. Many bugs live at the edges: empty input, one item, all equal.
The other options are more of the same kind of case.

try.task: Use the five steps on anagrams. On paper, do steps 1 to 4 first: what is the input, which examples (including empty strings), what is the brute force, what is the better way. Then write isAnagram(a, b): it returns true when both strings use exactly the same letters the same number of times.
try.hint: Brute force: sort both strings and compare. Better: count the letters of the first string in a Map, then subtract for the second string. Different lengths can never match.

takeaway.key: Do not code first: understand, write examples, state the brute force, improve it, then code and test.
mistakes: Starting to code before the task is clear.
Skipping edge-case examples such as empty input or one item.
Jumping to a clever trick without a brute-force baseline to compare with.
Finishing the code without running the examples through it.

dryRun.title: a starts as [3, 1, 2]
dryRun.note: Only sort and push changed a. slice and map left it alone and returned a new array.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
const b = a.reverse()
console.log(a[0], b[0])
why: reverse changes the original array and returns that same array. So a[0] and b[0] both read 3.
Trap: thinking b is a reversed copy.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
console.log(a.push(4), a.length)
why: push returns the new length, which is 4. It does not return the array.
Trap: writing const next = a.push(4) and expecting an array.

think.q:
const a = [[1], [2]]
const b = [...a]
b[0].push(9)
console.log(a[0].length)
why: Spread makes a shallow copy: the outer array is new, but the inner arrays are still shared. Pushing into b[0] also changes a[0].
For nested data, copy each level you change.
think.exec:
const a = [[1], [2]]
const b = [...a]
b[0].push(9)
console.log(a[0].length)

think.q: Which call gives you a new array and leaves a unchanged?
why: concat builds a new array. The others change a: reverse flips it, push adds to it, splice removes from it.
In React state, use the methods that return a new array.

think.q: console.log([10, 9, 1].sort().join(','))
why: Without a compare function, sort turns items into strings and sorts them as text. As text, "1" comes before "10", and "10" before "9".
Fix: sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers.

try.task: Write uniqueSorted(nums). Return a new array with the distinct numbers in ascending order. The input array must stay unchanged.
try.hint: new Set(nums) removes duplicates and [...set] makes an array. Then sort a copy with a number compare function.

checks.t: sorts as numbers, not as text

checks.verify: const a = [3, 1, 3]; uniqueSorted(a); assert(JSON.stringify(a) === "[3,1,3]", "input was changed")

takeaway.key: Know which methods change the array (push, sort, splice, reverse) and which return a new one (map, filter, slice, concat).
mistakes: Calling sort() on numbers without a compare function.
Expecting spread or slice to copy nested arrays too.
Changing React state arrays in place.
Assuming push returns the array. It returns the new length.

dryRun.title: Build "abcde" with s += c (counting the copying)
dryRun.note: Each step writes a whole new string, so the total is 1 + 2 + ... + n. For n = 5 that is already 15. Real engines often optimise this, but your analysis should assume the copy.

think.q:
let s = 'abc'
s.toUpperCase()
console.log(s)
why: Strings are immutable. toUpperCase returns a new string and leaves s alone. The result was thrown away.
Fix: s = s.toUpperCase().

think.q: console.log('banana'.indexOf('an'), 'banana'.lastIndexOf('an'))
why: "banana" is b-a-n-a-n-a. The text "an" first starts at index 1 and last starts at index 3.
Both methods return the start index of the match.

think.q: console.log('hello'.split('').sort().join(''))
why: split("") makes an array of letters, sort orders them as text, and join("") glues them back: "ehllo".
This sorted string is a handy key: all anagrams of a word give the same one.

think.q: You build a string of n characters with s += c in a loop. Analysed as "every append copies the whole string", the total work is:
why: The copies are 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is about n²/2. That is O(n²).
Fix: push the pieces into an array and call join("") once at the end: O(n).

think.q: console.log('😀'.length)
why: JavaScript counts UTF-16 code units, and an emoji takes two of them. So length is 2, not 1.
Be careful when a problem has emoji or rare symbols: use [...str] to walk real characters.

try.task: Write reverseWords(str). Return the words in reverse order, separated by a single space. Ignore extra spaces at the start, at the end and between words.
examples: reverseWords("the sky is blue")  // "blue is sky the"
try.hint: trim() removes the outer spaces. split(/\s+/) splits on any run of spaces. Then reverse() and join(" "). For an empty string, return an empty string.

checks.verify: assert(reverseWords("the sky is blue") === "blue is sky the", "wrong result")
assert(reverseWords("  hello   world ") === "world hello", "extra spaces must go")

takeaway.key: Strings are immutable: every change makes a new string, so build the pieces in an array and join once.
mistakes: Building a big string with += in a loop.
Expecting s[0] = "x" to change the string.
Calling a string method and ignoring the returned new string.
Trusting length for emoji and rare symbols.

dryRun.title: Pushing 8 items into an array that doubles when full (simplified model)
dryRun.note: Push 5 copies 4 items, but most pushes copy nothing. For all 8 pushes the copies add up to 7, fewer than 2 per push. That is why push is amortized O(1). This is a simplified model: real engines choose their own growth.

think.q:
const a = []
a[5] = 1
console.log(a.length)
why: length is always the highest index plus one. Writing at index 5 makes it 6, and indexes 0 to 4 become empty holes.
This shows that a JS array is not a fixed block: it grows when you write past its end.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
a.length = 0
console.log(a[0] === undefined, a.length)
why: Setting length = 0 empties the array. Reading any index now gives undefined.
It is a quick way to clear an array in place.
think.exec:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
a.length = 0
console.log(a[0] === undefined, a.length)

think.q: A resize copies every item, so why do we still call push amortized O(1)?
opts: Because the array grows by one slot at a time
Because resizes are rare: the capacity doubles, so n pushes copy only about 2n items in total
why: After a resize there is a lot of free room, so many pushes cost nothing extra. Spread over all pushes, the copying adds only a small constant per push.
Amortized means the average cost over many operations, with a guarantee, not luck.

think.q: Suppose the array grew by just one slot each time it was full. What would n pushes cost in total?
why: Every push would copy everything: 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is about n²/2. That is O(n²).
Doubling is what makes the total linear.

think.q: Which single call can cost O(n) in the worst case?
why: A push into a full array triggers a resize that copies all n items. Index access, length and pop never copy.
That is the difference between worst case (one call) and amortized (many calls).

try.task: Write countCopies(n). Simulate pushing n items into an array whose capacity starts at 1 and doubles when it is full. Return the total number of items copied during all the resizes.
try.hint: Keep cap, size and copies. Before each push, if size === cap, add size to copies and double cap. Then increase size.

takeaway.key: A dynamic array grows by doubling, so one push can cost O(n), but pushes are O(1) amortized.
mistakes: Calling push O(n) because of the occasional resize.
Imagining growth by a fixed amount: that would make n pushes O(n²).
Mixing up amortized cost with average-case luck.
Forgetting that inserting in the middle is still O(n).

flags: 5-step: the old text says "the interviewer is scoring you". I did not rewrite it, but the lesson rules say learning material should not use that framing.
strings: the += copying cost is a conceptual model. V8 often optimises it with ropes, so a benchmark may not show O(n²). The dry-run note says so.
static-dynamic-arrays: the doubling model is simplified. Real engines use their own growth factors, and the note says so.
